summary: Defines two ways to wrap an HMAC key for protection: one encrypts it with a Triple DES key and the other with an AES key. One use is the Authenticated Data type in the Cryptographic Message Syntax. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: A secret key sometimes has to be sent somewhere. This memo shows how to lock one key inside another key's protection while it travels.

questions: hmac key wrap with aes or 3des
how to wrap an hmac key with aes
how to wrap an hmac key with triple des
what is a key encryption key
subtitle: How to lock an HMAC key of any length inside a Triple-DES or AES key so it can be stored or sent safely.

tldr.problem: The existing Triple-DES and AES key wrap methods only handle keys of certain sizes (and 3DES wrap imposes parity rules), which makes it hard to wrap an HMAC key of arbitrary length.
tldr.mechanism: The HMAC key is prefixed with a one-octet length, padded to a multiple of 8 octets, and then wrapped with the 3DES algorithm of RFC 3217 (with a two-pass CBC step) or the AES key wrap algorithm of RFC 3394.
tldr.outcome: Two algorithm identifiers were assigned, one for HMAC key wrap with Triple-DES and one with AES, which the Cryptographic Message Syntax Authenticated Data type can use. The RFC is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 3537 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It builds on RFC 3217 and RFC 3394.

sections.title: The Problem: Wrapping a Key of Any Length
sections.content:
Key wrapping means encrypting one cryptographic key with another. The key doing the encrypting is the key-encryption key (KEK). Standard methods already exist for wrapping a Triple-DES (3DES) content-encryption key with a 3DES KEK (RFC 3217) and an AES content-encryption key with an AES KEK (RFC 3394).

Neither fits an HMAC key well. Triple-DES key wrap imposes parity restrictions, and both methods restrict the size of the key being wrapped. An HMAC key has no particular parity and can have a variable length.

RFC 3537 therefore specifies a way to encrypt an HMAC key of arbitrary length with either a 3DES KEK or an AES KEK. It uses the requirement words MUST, SHOULD and so on as defined in RFC 2119.
sections.eli5: There are already special boxes for locking up some kinds of keys, but they only fit keys of certain sizes. This memo makes a box that can fit a secret of any length.

sections.title: HMAC Key Guidelines
sections.content:
The memo starts with a short reminder from the HMAC specification (RFC 2104) about key size. The key should be at least as long as the output (called L) of the hash function in use.

When a key is longer than the block size of the hash algorithm, it is hashed first and the resulting hash value is used. Using keys much longer than L gives no security benefit, unless the random function used to create the key has low entropy output.

This is why the wrapping has to cope with many key lengths: HMAC keys are not a fixed size.
sections.eli5: A secret key should be about as long as the lock's answer, and making it much longer does not help. But people still use lots of different lengths, so the box has to fit them all.

sections.title: Wrapping with Triple-DES
sections.content:
The 3DES method is based on the algorithm in Section 3 of RFC 3217, changed because an HMAC key is variable length and has no parity. The steps for wrapping are:

  • Call the HMAC key KEY and its length in octets LENGTH, which is a single octet. Form LKEY = LENGTH || KEY.
  • Add PAD, the fewest random octets needed to make the total a multiple of 8 octets (zero if it already is). The result is LKEYPAD.
  • Compute an 8 octet key checksum on LKEYPAD as described in RFC 3217, call it ICV, and append it to get LKEYPADICV.
  • Generate 8 random octets as IV and encrypt LKEYPADICV in CBC mode with the 3DES KEK. Call the ciphertext TEMP1.
  • Form TEMP2 = IV || TEMP1, reverse the order of its octets to get TEMP3, and encrypt TEMP3 in CBC mode with the KEK using the fixed initialization vector 0x4adda22c79e82105.

Unwrapping runs the steps in reverse. It must reject a wrapped key that is not a multiple of 8 octets, a checksum that does not match, and a PAD longer than 7 octets. When the same HMAC key is wrapped under different 3DES KEKs, a fresh IV must be generated each time.
sections.eli5: You write down how long the secret is, add some filler so it fits neatly, add a check number, then scramble it twice, flipping it backwards in between. To open it, you do everything backwards and check the numbers match.

sections.title: Wrapping with AES
sections.content:
The AES method reuses the AES key wrap algorithm of RFC 3394 and differs only by adding padding, since an HMAC key length may not be a multiple of 64 bits. Wrapping builds LKEYPAD exactly as in the 3DES case (a length octet, the key, then 0 to 7 random pad octets) and then encrypts it with the AES key wrap algorithm using the AES KEK. The result is 8 octets longer than LKEYPAD.

Unwrapping rejects a wrapped key that is not a multiple of 8 octets, runs the AES key unwrap algorithm and fails if its internal integrity check fails, then splits out LENGTH, KEY and PAD. A PAD of more than 7 octets is an error. Otherwise KEY is used as the HMAC key.

This is simpler than the 3DES method because the AES algorithm already has its own integrity check, so no separate checksum or double encryption is needed.
sections.eli5: With AES the strong box already has a built-in seal that tells you if it was tampered with. You only need to add the length note and some filler before you lock it.

sections.title: Algorithm Identifiers
sections.content:
Protocols that use ASN.1 name their cryptographic algorithms with object identifiers. The memo assigns two, one for each method. In both cases the AlgorithmIdentifier parameter field MUST be NULL.

  • id-alg-HMACwith3DESwrap is { iso(1) member-body(2) us(840) rsadsi(113549) pkcs(1) pkcs-9(9) smime(16) alg(3) 11 }.
  • id-alg-HMACwithAESwrap is { iso(1) member-body(2) us(840) rsadsi(113549) pkcs(1) pkcs-9(9) smime(16) alg(3) 12 }.

The abstract names one place such an algorithm is used: the Authenticated Data type in the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS).
sections.eli5: Each kind of box gets its own name tag so the two sides of a conversation can say which box they used. The tags are a long number made of small parts, and the last part tells the boxes apart.

sections.title: Test Vectors
sections.content:
The RFC gives one worked example for each method so implementers can check their code. Both use the same KEK, 5840df6e 29b02af1 ab493b70 5bf16ea1 ae8338f4 dcc176a8, and the same HMAC key, c37b7e64 92584340 bed12207 80894115 5068f738.

For 3DES, the example lists the random IV (050d8c79 e0d56b75), the PAD (38be62), the ICV and every intermediate value up to the final wrapped key. For AES, the pad is 050d8c and the wrapped key is shown in full. The values are given in full in the RFC.
sections.eli5: The memo includes a worked example with all the numbers filled in, like an answer key, so people building their own can check they got the same result.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementations must protect the KEK. If it is compromised, every HMAC key wrapped with it may be disclosed, which may lead to loss of data integrity protection.

Wrapping provides confidentiality and data integrity but not necessarily data origination authentication, because anyone holding the KEK can create a message that passes the integrity check. If origin authentication is wanted, the KEK distribution mechanism must provide it, or a digital signature may be used.

Implementations must generate IVs and padding randomly, and the RFC warns that good random numbers are difficult to produce, pointing to RFC 1750. Finally, the algorithms have been reviewed only for use with Triple-DES and AES, not other encryption algorithms.
sections.eli5: If someone steals the key that makes the strong box, they can open every box made with it, so guard it well. Also, the box shows nothing was tampered with, but not who packed it.
